PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 68 — Lesson 92: Type 2 Diabetes Management

FNP-level goal: Turn a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes into a safe, individualized longitudinal plan: confirm the clinical context, set patient-centered goals, select treatment by benefit and risk, prevent complications, monitor response, and know when urgent or specialty care is needed.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish diagnosis, monitoring, and acute evaluation in diabetes care.
  • Set individualized glycemic goals using comorbidity, hypoglycemia risk, life expectancy, treatment burden, and patient priorities.
  • Choose lifestyle and medication strategies using kidney, heart, weight, cost, access, and safety context.
  • Recognize hypoglycemia, hyperglycemic crises, and illness-related escalation.
  • Build a complication-prevention and follow-up plan with clear ownership.

Part 1 — Diabetes Care Is Risk Management

Type 2 diabetes management is not simply “lower the A1c.” It includes symptoms, glucose trends, hypoglycemia risk, blood pressure, kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, weight, medication access, nutrition, activity, mental health, pregnancy potential when relevant, and the patient’s goals. Verify diagnosis and current status using appropriate current criteria and repeat/confirm results when indicated.

Part 2 — Individualize the Goal

Glycemic goals should be individualized. A patient with long life expectancy and low hypoglycemia risk may benefit from a different target than a frail older adult with recurrent hypoglycemia, advanced comorbidity, limited support, or high treatment burden. Discuss what the patient can realistically monitor and what outcomes matter: symptoms, energy, avoiding hypoglycemia, kidney/heart protection, weight, and prevention of long-term complications.

Part 3 — Choose Treatment by the Whole Patient

Lifestyle support should be specific and feasible: nutrition pattern, food access, activity, sleep, tobacco/nicotine, alcohol, stress, and weight goals. Medication choice requires current guideline review and patient factors: ASCVD/heart failure/CKD, renal and hepatic function, hypoglycemia risk, weight effect, route, adverse effects, interactions, pregnancy potential, cost, coverage, and ability to use the treatment correctly.

Do not prescribe from an A1c alone. Explain why each treatment is used, how to take it, expected benefit, important adverse effects, sick-day/illness instructions when appropriate, monitoring, and follow-up. Teach-back and device demonstration are essential for injectable therapies and glucose monitoring.

Part 4 — Hypoglycemia and Hyperglycemia Safety

Hypoglycemia risk rises with some therapies, missed meals, exercise changes, alcohol, renal decline, dosing errors, and limited food access. Symptoms may include sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, confusion, behavior change, seizure, or loss of consciousness. Severe symptoms or inability to self-treat require emergency help. Review prevention, recognition, immediate action, and who can assist.

Marked hyperglycemia with vomiting, dehydration, abdominal pain, altered mental status, rapid/deep breathing, severe weakness, or inability to keep fluids down may represent an acute metabolic emergency. Do not manage a potentially unstable patient by portal message alone; use urgent/emergency evaluation according to presentation.

Part 5 — Prevent Complications and Close Loops

Use a coordinated plan for blood pressure, lipid/CV risk, kidney function and albuminuria when indicated, foot symptoms/examination, eye care, neuropathy, oral health, vaccines, tobacco cessation, and mental-health/substance-use needs. Screening is not complete until results are reviewed and follow-up occurs. New foot ulceration, infection, ischemic change, severe neuropathic symptoms, rapidly declining renal function, or visual change may require urgent specialty or emergency pathways.

Clinical Case

A 63-year-old with diabetes, CKD, heart failure, food insecurity, and several missed doses reports dizziness and intermittent low readings. The FNP should not merely intensify medication. Reconcile actual use, assess hypoglycemia and volume status, review kidney/heart risk, food access, monitoring technique, and medication contributors; then build an accessible plan with clear follow-up and escalation instructions.

FNP Diabetes Framework

  1. Assess now: symptoms, acute instability, glucose pattern, medicines, food access, and self-management capacity.
  2. Individualize goals: benefits, harms, hypoglycemia risk, comorbidities, and patient priorities.
  3. Select treatment: use current evidence plus heart/kidney, weight, renal, access, and safety context.
  4. Teach and monitor: device technique, adverse effects, illness plan, labs, trends, and follow-up.
  5. Prevent complications: CV, renal, retinal, neurologic, foot, and psychosocial care with closed-loop referrals/results.

High-Yield Summary

Diabetes care: is individualized risk reduction, not an A1c number alone.
Medication choice: depends on heart/kidney disease, hypoglycemia, weight, renal function, access, and patient preference.
Hypoglycemia: can be life-threatening; assess food, dosing, renal function, and treatment risks.
Acute hyperglycemia: with systemic symptoms may require emergency assessment.
FNP standard: create a feasible plan with monitoring, complication prevention, clear ownership, and escalation instructions.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Diagnostic criteria, glycemic targets, medication selection, pregnancy considerations, sick-day plans, monitoring, referral, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, local policy, scope, and the individual patient’s presentation.
